source.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of LLM Jailbreaks via Internal Attribution Graphs
source.authors: Anupam Wagle; Ifrat Ikhtear Uddin; Chao-Wei Zhang; Long-Wei Wang

page_placements.theme: Attribution graphs and circuits: own-unit circuits vs replacement models with error terms

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests graph-based explanations of model behavior using transcoder features, but reports that top-feature ablations do not restore refusals and that omitting reconstruction-error nodes greatly worsens reconstruction fidelity. These results qualify the sufficiency of feature-level attribution graphs.
record.gate_note: The study does not audit neuron poles or score explanations against held-out activating examples. Relevant results are its graph-metric associations with jailbreak outcomes, the layer-depth comparison, reconstruction-fidelity ablation, and feature-ablation intervention. The reported attribution graphs use trained transcoders and reconstruction-error nodes, not only the model's own neurons.
record.test_reason: The study builds attribution graphs from trained per-layer transcoder features plus reconstruction-error nodes, not from the model's own neurons, to diagnose jailbreaks in Llama-2-7B-chat. It reports only how its own graph metrics relate to attack success, plus reconstruction fidelity and feature ablations. None of this measures whether native-neuron graphs explain behaviour without a replacement model (V5). It does not audit neuron poles (V1, V2), vision neurons (V3, V4) or explanation scoring (V6, V7). The record's V5 link and its three V5 labels are therefore unfounded.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that path rerouting in layers 0–5 correlates with jailbreak success (r=0.461) while static metrics do not. They add that this signal is concentrated in semantic-bridging attacks (r=0.865 within context switching) and weakens at layers 0–15, which they attribute to transcoder quality. They read the failed top-3 feature ablations as evidence of distributed, redundant computation. The abstract's claims of 'multiple open-source LLMs' and that interventions 'improve model robustness' contradict the body: only Llama-2-7B-chat is analysed, and 0/4 interventions succeeded.
record.recipe_differences: The study builds paired attribution graphs from trained per-layer transcoder features, includes reconstruction-error nodes, and analyzes jailbreak prompts; it does not audit neuron poles or use the original neuron-explanation evaluation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The path-rerouting correlation weakened when graph coverage increased from layers 0–5 to 0–15; the authors attribute this to lower transcoder quality in some intermediate layers.

fits_no_version.finding: In Llama-2-7B-chat, the transcoder-based attribution graph matches model outputs only with error nodes (KL 0.0014). Without them, KL is 46.96.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Replacement-model (transcoder) attribution graphs depend on reconstruction-error terms for faithfulness. This is the cost V5's native-neuron approach claims to avoid, but no neuron-only comparison was run.

fits_no_version.finding: Zero-ablating the top-3 emergent transcoder features restored refusal in 0 of 4 successful jailbreaks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Top-activation features in transcoder graphs are not individually causally sufficient for jailbreak behaviour; effects appear distributed.

record.code_released: The paper says code and a sample dataset are included in supplementary material; URL not stated.
record.problems: The main analysis has 30 prompt pairs and only 4 successful attacks. The study reports that path-rerouting results are sensitive to graph depth and transcoder quality. Its intervention experiment tests only top-3 feature ablations, and the reported ablations do not restore refusal.

untested.parts: All: no neuron-pole audit of Qwen3-32B or any model.
All: no neuron-share audits across models or scales. Pythia-6.9B appears only in transcoder reconstruction metrics.
All: no vision models, no InceptionV1, no pose or recursive generalization.
All: no interpretable-neuron shares as a function of architecture, regularization or tools.
All: no attribution graph built from the model's native neurons; graphs use trained transcoders with error nodes.
All: no comparison of explanation fit on activating examples against held-out prediction.
All: no simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The record over-links rows to V5. The study never builds neuron-based graphs; its nodes are trained transcoder features with error nodes, so it cannot bear on whether native neurons suffice. All verdict labels are removed. The relation is set to uses_without_test/T4 because it applies attribution-graph circuit methodology as a tool and reports its own method's performance. It does not cite the 'already clean' essay. There are internal inconsistencies: the abstract versus the results, and 'first ten layers' versus layers 0–5. The N=500 extension shows the metrics degenerate on topic-decoupled pairs.

versions.untested_parts: Neuron-pole job counts, including one-job, two-related-job, and not-understood shares.
Neuron-pole shares across models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, or scales up to trillions of parameters. Pythia-6.9B appears only in transcoder reconstruction-quality results.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, and recursive generalization.
Architecture, regularization, tool improvements, and interpretability-share estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.

The study uses trained transcoder features and reconstruction-error nodes, not graphs made only from native neurons without a trained replacement or its reconstruction error. It tests top-feature ablation, not comprehensive neuron-level causal sufficiency.
Explanation fit on activating examples versus prediction on separate activations.
Automated explanation scoring by simulating activations on new text.

relation.reason: The study does not use the neurons-already-clean finding. It uses transcoders, not neurons, and never mentions neuron interpretability or the essay. cites_only is the weakest of the available values; strictly, the study does not cite the claim at all.

tranche.reason: T4 means the study uses the finding as a tool. This study builds its graphs from trained per-layer transcoder features plus error nodes, which is the replacement-model approach that V5 says is unnecessary. It never uses native neurons as units and never audits neurons, so it neither tests nor uses the finding.

source_check.notes: Table 3 (N=10, Llama-2-7B-chat-hf, the only model in the main experiments per Sec 4.1) shows the transcoder graph is unfaithful without error nodes. No neuron-based graph is built, so this does not test V5. Sec 4.1 gives a different with-error-node figure (mean KL 0.0027, top-1 99.2%) from Table 3's 0.0014. The conclusion calls the graphs 'sparse autoencoder-based', but the method trains transcoders.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Path rerouting in layers 0–5 on the 30-pair main analysis
reader_labels.reason: Path rerouting correlated with attack success (R5), though this is an association and does not establish a complete causal explanation.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Graph metrics across layers 0–15 and static metrics in the reported analyses
reader_labels.reason: Most graph metrics were not significantly associated with attack success, and the path-rerouting association weakened at greater depth (R1–R4, R6–R9).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: No-error-node reconstruction and top-3 feature ablation
reader_labels.reason: Removing error nodes produced much higher reconstruction KL, and top-3 feature ablations restored refusal in none of the four successful attacks (R10, R12).
